blocks.html: Every dog in the program follows the same five-phase development system, built around one principle: drive and self-control are developed separately, then brought together deliberately. Rushing that order is the most common mistake in this industry, and it's the one that produces dogs that look impressive in a demonstration and fall apart the first time real life doesn't follow the script.

Development begins in the first days of life. Early handling and controlled stimulation build a stronger foundation for later environmental confidence and stress resilience. Structured early handling exercises here build a foundation for stress resilience later in life, alongside controlled exposure to textures, surfaces, and sensory experiences, and continuous evaluation of genetic expression and aptitude.

Structured exposure to people, animals, and environments during this critical period develops confident, stable dogs capable of functioning across diverse settings — systematic exposure to different surfaces, sounds, and scenarios, plus early foundation work relevant to specialized detection capability.

This phase establishes core obedience and introduces foundational protection concepts — reliable command response across environments, and channeling genetic drive into focused, usable working capability rather than raw intensity.

Work becomes progressively more demanding through varied people, locations, surfaces, distractions, and pressure. The purpose isn't to make the dog more aggressive — it's to test whether the dog can keep thinking as the difficulty increases. A dog that only performs when everything is predictable hasn't actually learned the job.

The final phase is about proving the dog consistently, honestly identifying any remaining weaknesses, and teaching the future handler how to maintain the work correctly. A protection dog that arrives without proper handler training is a liability, not an asset — this step isn't optional.

Every dog in the program follows this same core standard — there are no lower or higher training tiers. Once a dog is matched with a future handler, later work can be adapted to that person's environment and needs. The standard underneath it doesn't change.
